analysis.one_liner: Requires the President to declare a climate emergency and steer federal investment toward clean energy and disadvantaged communities.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in March 2021, was never taken up, and died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the President to formally declare a national emergency over climate change and then direct the federal government to spend on large projects: rebuilding public infrastructure, retrofitting millions of homes and schools, expanding clean energy manufacturing, and protecting farmland and forests. At least 40% of the money would have to go to historically disadvantaged communities, projects would have to meet union-level labor standards, and the bill bars privatizing public land or water. It also calls for new New Deal-style public institutions to channel the investment.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and low-income communities would get the direct gains: the bill requires family-sustaining wages, workplace safety, and union organizing rights on every project, and reserves at least 40% of investment for historically disadvantaged communities. Homeowners, schools, and public agencies would benefit from retrofits that cut energy bills and pollution, and rural communities and farmers get regenerative agriculture and local food system investment.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President to declare a national climate emergency and direct federal investment in mitigation and resiliency projects, with at least 40% of the investment going to historically disadvantaged communities.

Directs projects to conform to labor standards providing family-sustaining wages, safe workplaces, and protection of workers' rights to organize, and bars projects that would decrease union density or membership.

Targets upgrades to public infrastructure — clean energy, transportation, high-speed broadband, and water — with a focus on public systems, and modernizes and retrofits millions of homes, schools, offices, and industrial buildings to reduce pollution and energy costs.

Requires reinvestment in existing public sector institutions and creation of new ones, on the New Deal model, to channel investment at the pace the emergency requires, and prohibits projects that privatize public land, public water, or natural resources.

analysis.who_pays: The cost of the mobilization would fall on the federal budget — the bill specifies no funding source, so taxpayers would bear whatever Congress appropriates. Fossil fuel producers and utilities would face an economy steered away from oil, gas, and coal, which the bill's findings describe as an 'economically just phase-out' needed to keep carbon in the ground.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the President to declare a national emergency under the National Emergencies Act, a legal framework that unlocks sweeping executive powers with only an annual report to Congress as an ongoing check; opponents argue emergency declarations should be limited to foreign or acute crises, not used as a standing tool for domestic economic policy.

The bill directs large-scale federal investment but contains no funding mechanism, no spending total, and no pay-for, leaving the full cost of the mobilization to future Congresses to finance or leave unfunded.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it targets, the benefits are large and concrete: union-wage jobs, cheaper energy from retrofitted buildings, and a mandated share of investment for communities that usually get left out. The honest objections are about design, not purpose — the emergency-declaration route concentrates sweeping power in the executive branch, and the bill orders a massive mobilization without saying how it would be paid for. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much one trusts future administrations to use the powers as the bill intends.

outcome.mechanism: Bernie Sanders introduced it in March 2021 and the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never took it up, so it sat untouched until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on March 23, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — and the Congress ended January 3, 2023, without the bill advancing.
Four Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and anyone opposed to large-scale public energy investment are better off, because the bill never even reached a committee vote, let alone the floor. The communities and workers the bill targeted gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel interests; no vote ever happened

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring a presidential climate emergency declaration and a federally directed climate mobilization.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill; it received only a referral and no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule the bill for committee action at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No Republican supported the bill, and Democratic support was thin — only 4 of 48 Senate Democrats signed on — with no vote ever taken.

industries.note: The bill's findings call for an economically just phase-out of oil, gas, and coal, and its emergency mobilization would steer federal investment away from fossil fuels. Its death left the industry's position unchanged.
Retrofitting millions of buildings and public infrastructure under required family-sustaining wages and organizing protections would have been a major jobs program for union labor.

The bill prioritizes domestic manufacturing of clean energy technologies and public clean-energy infrastructure, creating demand for these firms — with a public-sector focus rather than pure private subsidy.

The bill directs a particular focus on public systems for energy, transportation, broadband, and water, favoring public provision over the privately owned utilities that now control most of that infrastructure.
